utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So paragraph 82 as written is a little bit confusing. Now, with respect to the RJB, the -- pardon me, the public security department --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only roughly dealt with the MUP, I didn't go into detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Now, with respect to the RJB you mentions SUPs and OUPs, and in fact you don't mention [Interpretation] Police station [In English] or their relationship to SUPs or OUPs. Would you agree that that the structure of the MUP is a topic that you did not have sufficient knowledge about to form an expert opinion for purposes of this report and that the information presented is a simplification of a very complex ministerial organ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By definition I accept any critique of whatever I have authored, including yours. Of course I have no ambition of saying that I have encompassed everything, but I don't think your conclusion is quite justified. I didn't speak of the five operative administrations of the MUP or the other accompanying administrations or about the units of PJP. I only mentioned what I thought sufficient to explain the command competence of General Ojdanic. I did not deal with the MUP as such, but I appreciate your comment that I'm not an expert in the MUP and I'm not competent to judge every one of its elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm just making sure -- I think the transcript is completed. With respect to what you have written about, you have just mentioned the existence of the MUP staff in Pristina in paragraph 86. Would you agree with me that you were not able to offer any opinions as to the functioning of this organ or its interaction with other MUP structures based upon the information contained in your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And likewise, you have also mentioned -- you have a diagram at two places, on pages 124 you have a diagram that places the state security department under the MUP staff for Kosovo. Would the same -- would the same fact apply to this representation -- well, strike that. Let me ask you a different question. Would you agree with me that the -- based upon your knowledge of the MUP, the state security department is separate and apart from the public security department of the MUP or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and with respect to the -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, with your leave, page 46, line 25, witness said: I did not deal with the MUP as such, but I appreciate your comment that I'm not an expert in the MUP and I'm not competent to judge every one its elements. And he added: [Interpretation] But I can speak to what I'm testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's why I'm going through the precise paragraphs that the witness mentions the MUP in clarifying --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- The extent of his knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, General, if we can return to the chart on page 124, the diagram mistakenly places the state security department under the MUP staff, which was an RJB organ. Would you agree that you cannot, based upon the information you have, form an opinion as to the -- as to its nature, that the RJB would be in charge of the RDB in essence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are only partially right. I can tell you how I drew that conclusion that underlies this diagram. You have the founding act of the MUP staff for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, and there is a whole series of those documents dating from 1996 to 1998. In this founding act, there are tasks of the staff listed, the staff for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. And you will see that one of their tasks was to plan, organize, supervise, and control the forces involved in anti-terrorist combat in Kosovo and Metohija and the units that were brought into Kosovo and Metohija. It is quite certain that units for special operations took part in anti-terrorist struggle, and it is beyond any doubt that as part of that anti-terrorist struggle they were under the control of the MUP or at least should have been. I see no other way to explain it than the way I explained it. Of course the sector of state security does not fall under the sector of public security, that's quite clear. But that's why the staff of the MUP was established for the anti-terrorist struggle, in order to plan, organize, and control all the forces involved in that struggle. For instance, the -- whether the staff controlled the JSO, I don't know, I didn't deal with it and I have no information how it functioned on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I had to wait for the translation and the transcript. So essentially your conclusions are based solely on the decision on the formation of the staff, and you do not know how and to what extent that was actually realised in reality on the terrain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have combat reports of units for special operations, so I could not establish that. I concluded this on the basis of the founding document and the establishment of the staff and giving the staff a mandate in this founding document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General Professor, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, very few, Your Honour. It won't take very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm John Ackerman, I represent General Pavkovic in this case. I assume you have your report in front of you and it might not be important whether you do or not. I want to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in my bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you need to refer to it, please feel free. Page 117 you're talking about, it's paragraph 159 of your report, I believe. And you may want to look at it if you can get it out of your bag and look. It may help you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it's paragraph 159, it's on page 119 of my copy, Mr. Ackerman. Perhaps that's done with printing. I think the best way to deal with this to avoid confusion is to refer to the paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that sometimes gets confusing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it does but there are two sections and two lots of paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll get it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's paragraph 159 and the footnote is 205, and I'm interested in the comments you make in the footnote where you say this: "Not only was this no longer featuring in the combat report of the 3rd Army, but the 3rd Army commander did not complain to the president at the meeting held on 4th or 5th May at which he and General Lukic reported." I'd like to know the source of your information about this meeting that happened on the 4th or the 5th of May with General Pavkovic, General Lukic, and apparently Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment I really cannot recall the source. In the transcript from evening briefings, maybe -- well, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that General Ojdanic was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that General Ojdanic should have been present at the meeting, but I'm telling you, really, at this point in time I cannot recall. And during the course of the afternoon, I'll look it up. In my hotel room I have some more papers, and then I'll look it up and tomorrow then I can tell you, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. You can just let us know tomorrow if you find anything out about it. You'll remember the document 3D670, that's the 18 April Milosevic resubordination order. I don't think we need to look at it again. What I want to ask you is: Do you have any knowledge that anybody within the MUP organization ever received a copy of that order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the course of your investigations into these matters, did you ever find one document where the MUP reported to the VJ as if they were actually subordinated to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at another document, it's P2594, and I want to look at paragraph 45 of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, that document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I was just getting ready to ask about, I think it is. So what do we need to do, go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think for security sake we should go into private session while we deal with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The document number for the exhibit now being deal with is P2600.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if you -- I know you did, you had an opportunity to review this document in preparing your report because you refer to it in footnote 206 of your report, in fact you refer to this paragraph. The paragraph is a bit long, but it describes the progress of the efforts to resubordinate MUP to the VJ. And this is General Vasiljevic's statement where he talking about that process. He talks about the order of Milosevic which was ordered, he talks about Pavkovic's complaint in writing that the subordination had not occurred, that as a result of that Ojdanic went to Milosevic, and Milosevic said MUP would be confronted but that he shouldn't be too concerned because the problems with resubordination were more to deal with Montenegro than Kosovo. And then he says this: "I'm aware of this exchange as Ojdanic showed me his personal notes on the matter." Did you also get a chance to see those personal notes and confirm that what General Vasiljevic is saying here is correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Finally I'd like you to look then at another document, it's 4D0299. And during the examination of Mr. Ivetic there was some confusion, I think, or at least some question about the dates regarding these resubordination orders and when it was decreed that MUP should actually resubordinate itself to the VJ. So what I want you to look at is General Pavkovic's order, which was based upon General Ojdanic's order in that regard. And I suggest to you that nowhere in that order does General Pavkovic set out a date by which that resubordination should occur, does he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was a question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is not mentioned by which the resubordination has to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that when General Lazarevic issued his order saying that there should be a resubordination of specific MUP units by the 25th of April, it makes sense, doesn't it, that he was referring to a resubordination that had to occur under the terms of Article 17 of the Law on Defence for an upcoming action that would be taking place on the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 180, this is a completely different subject now of your report, you talk about the training that members and officers of the VJ would go through in the international law of war and other things. And one of the schools you talk about is called the School of National Defence, which is the highest level providing advanced education to commanding officers. And you tell us that that School of National Defence is for training these high-level commanding officers for commanding strategic groups, operations units, and for work in the General Staff and the Ministry of Defence, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So work of a highest-level -- assignment of a highest-level commanding officer to the Ministry of Defence was not an unusual assignment for someone in the higher ranks of the VJ, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. I really am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Assignment of a superior officer, a highly advanced officer, who went through this School of National Defence, an assignment of them to a position with the Ministry of Defence was a serious assignment, it was a -- it was one of the jobs that these high-ranking professionals in the army were assigned to on occasion, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the organization and formation of the Ministry of Defence, it is envisaged by establishment what job vacancies should be filled by officers who completed highest military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the assignment of someone to the Ministry of Defence is not a demotion or putting them out to pasture or anything like that, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. Well, I was in the Ministry of Defence too, and I did not consider that to being a demotion or having my role marginalised in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph, another subject now, 233 of your report you're talking about paramilitary organization and activity and its prevention. And in there you talk about -- I'll just read you the -- it's at the end of paragraph 233. "In addition today but not so reliably during the war, it is known that certain armed groups of former paramilitary units became part of the MUP and operated in Kosovo and Metohija, such were the Skorpioni and Arkanova." And then you say this: "Members of these units are being tried before the special court for war crimes in Belgrade for crimes committed in Podujevo." I want to ask you if you are aware as you sit here today that one of those persons, Sasa Cvjetan has actually been convicted by that court and sentenced to a 20-year prison sentence for killings that he was involved in with that unit in Podujevo? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that from the public domain in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want you to look at Exhibit P01811, please. Now, this is a document dated the 31st of May, 1999, it's from the Ministry of the Interior and it's called: "A decision on the establishment of the ministry staff for the suppression of terrorism." Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you said yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you explain this document to us? Does this look like a -- a MUP that is subordinated to the VJ or is this a MUP that is not subordinated to the VJ or does this have anything to do with that issue?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document has nothing to do with resubordination of the MUP to the Army of Yugoslavia because it was done with a view to having a separate organ for planning, organization, and supervising the anti-terrorist struggle of the forces of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what does this document tell us with regard to the issue of resubordination? Does it show that the MUP and VJ were each operating within their own separate chains of command? Is that what this suggests to us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document only indicates that a staff was established, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Stamp, do you wish to start or do you wish to leave it until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could, with your leave, leave it until tomorrow I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, Professor General, I have a few queries to make for purposes of clarifying my own mind about the issues which have come up in our report and through your testimony. Now, I feel that the issue of resubordination of MUP has been so much confused, firstly because we do not know whether the orders given by the president or the supreme commander with respect to the resubordination issue, whether these -- resubordination issue, whether these permeated below to MUP for purposes of compliance or not. And we see that MUP is functioning together with VJ in some areas. And we also see some correspondence at the lower echelons being exchanged between MUP and VJ or coming -- originating from VJ or sometimes from MUP in the language of the army. And then we also see that you have made some omissions in your report with respect to the placement of MUP forces alongside VJ during the combat period. Now, I think it was essential for the report that you had discovered why this was -- why there was such a confusion and what was happening, because after all a letter of the president seems never to have been officially received, and why there was no action over that. I mean, analysis on this was very essential and I would therefore request you to please argument your report with this answer so that this may clarify certain positions. I'm very grateful for your patience.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge, there are quite a few subquestions involved in our question, so I'm afraid that I may omit to answer some of them. So please do bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the MUP and the army are, no doubt, two separate systems and every one of them has their own chain of command and their own line of functioning, as it were, where they mind themselves at the same task and the struggle against terrorism was the same task for the army and the police except that every one of these systems does this in accordance with their own equipment, training, their level of training. Even if there had been no orders, people, commanders, commanding officers, people in the field, on the ground will establish some kind of cooperation, coordination, et cetera. As you could see, quite a few documents were shown to me here that this was actually the case, at brigade level and even in the case of the Pristina Corps. That is one undeniable fact. Also this cooperation between the army and the police in combatting terrorism started significantly before the month of July. We even have records stating that it began at the very beginning of 1998, as a matter of fact. There was coordination actions in concert between the army and the MUP even before the 28th of July, because according to the rules of service the army is authorised to react to terrorist strikes on the basis of self-defence. So the General Staff and military officers are duty-bound to react to all acts of terrorism. So there is one group of facts that can be established, namely, that at these levels down there, there was coordination, cooperation, coordinated action, regardless of whether there were orders coming from above or not because necessity made it incumbent on them to cooperate. There is also another group of facts, it seems to me that it was established beyond any doubt that the highest order from the very top, from the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, for the resubordination of the MUP, namely, those parts that are in the areas where combat activities are carried out, this did not go down the vertical chain of command of the MUP, to the MUP units. We have quite a few documents from the system of command of the army to that effect and also from the reports of the control concerning the situation on the ground, also from evening briefings, collegium meetings, there's quite a bit of information confirming that; that is to say there is no doubt about that, that this order did not get down the MUP chain of command. Now, why it did not arrive, I really have no answer to that. I think that it had to have arrived. And I think it is the military cabinet of the head of state that went astray there. They should have submitted this to the Government of Serbia, and then the Government of Serbia to the minister of interior, and then they down their own chain of command. I can only state that that was not done and it should have been done. Now, have I omitted to answer anything else? I'm here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your clarifications, but obviously when military and MUP were cooperating because of, as you said, national necessity, that's one thing. That is an obligation which was being felt and which was being -- I mean, fulfilled. But the problem really arose when there were incidents of indiscipline, when there was insubordination coming from certain areas of MUP and so on and so forth. So if the order had permeated or would have been followed up, perhaps it would have been the law then because of the presidential decree. But why this happened in such a situation where MUP and VJ were, as you said in your theory, were required to coordinate? But do you think it was a sabotage or it was something purposeful that this document never reached and just -- it went away like ether, thank you, volatile like ether, I mean. Thanks a lot, General. Could you kindly comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was sabotage of any kind. This is really speculation now. I mean, I have no arguments for this, but I think that rather it is a question of bickering between the two systems in the following way: The MUP never wanted the army to command them and it was the other way around, too. So I can understand it from that point of view, that it was this kind of bickering that did not allow the system of resubordination to function fully. However, there is yet another thing that I would like you to bear in mind in this context. Even if the resubordination had been fully been carried out, it does not pertain to the overall activity of the MUP, but only the participation of the MUP in the combat activities carried out by the military in the field specifically, and that lasts for as long as the action lasts. When the action is over, then the resubordination is suspended. So resubordination does not pertain to the entire time of the war, but only when combat activities are carried out and only within the framework of these combat activities. However, most of the MUP remains completely outside this subordination, even if the order had arrived. So if your question implies what the effects were of the lack of resubordination, it can only pertain to conduct within combat activities, not outside that. All the consequences that could have occurred outside combat activity would have taken place even if the resubordination had been carried through on orders from the head of state who acts in accordance with Article 17 of the Law on Defence that specifically states what this pertains to, combat activities that are organized and commanded by the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thanks a lot, but the question again would be that we quite understand that of course MUP was required to be a subordinate of VJ only for a specific purpose, to fight -- to join in the combats against terrorism, and we have the constitutional backing also for that and there is also the presidential letter. Then why bickering? Why was there indiscipline amongst these two discipline forces? Because if it is a presidential decree and if there is a constitutional authority for that purpose, then everybody should be bowed their heads to that. Why was there indiscipline? Why was this happening? Did you analyse this? Why at all was there such a situation in such a tense time, when as we go to your theories there was need for a national consensus on things? Thank you, General, could you say something on that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unable to deal with the causes of this. All I was able to deal with within the tasks sent to me for this expert report was whether it occurred or not. My duty ended there. The entire problem can be discussed at length in order to attempt to arrive at an answer to the question of why this happened. I didn't deal with that question, but from the large number of documents at my disposal I realised that it did not happen overall, only at the lower levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But then I feel that this report is destitute of certain essential facts which would have been very useful has the analysis been that complete even it could have been done briefly and we have not been able to find the cause and the effect reflected in the report. And my feeling is that this report is destitute of such essential information. Why was that left out? I mean, that's very surprising when you were looking at various causes. Thanks a lot, sir. I'm most grateful for your comments on my questions, I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, why do you think the order was made at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the order was made with the best of intentions, to unify the efforts of all the defence forces and the MUP and the army are the most prepared to carry out the tasks that had to be carried out in Kosovo at the time, so this was an effort to unify all the action taken to defend the country and in order to bring about a closer link between the army and the MUP in combat activities. I'm not saying this would have solved all the problems, but it would have been better if it had happened. And of course under the constitution this was also bound to be issued by the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's my question. Are you saying it was bound to be issued by the president? Once a state of war had been declared, did Articles 16 and 17 not apply automatically?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Articles 16 and 17 ought to have been applied automatically, but orders had to be issued to all systems to carry out resubordination. This had to be solved by certain documents of command; without those, there would be no resubordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's assume that Milosevic had every issued any order on this and General Lazarevic had decided that a particular combat operation required cooperation between the MUP and the VJ, with the MUP having the most directly involvement in the operation but the VJ providing support. Is he not automatically entitled, if he has instructions for such an operation, to engage the MUP forces under his command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the appropriate MUP unit would have to receive an order from its own chain of command to be resubordinated to the army in that operation; without such an order, it would not be resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that could, in theory, happen without Milosevic ever making any order as long as the MUP organs were cooperating with the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that resubordination was not carried out in full, I did not reach the conclusion that the MUP did not cooperate with the VJ. We are drawing a distinction here between cooperation, coordination, and command. Article 17 and the order of the president of the FRY meant that the MUP commanders who were in the areas of combat operations should be resubordinated to the military commanders, receive orders from them, and answer to them. That's a higher degree of cooperation than if cooperation is carried out by agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying then that the fact that the order was made by Milosevic removed the need for the resubordinated MUP organ to receive an order through its own chain of command? In the example I've given you, assuming the Milosevic order was made, would that then entitle General Lazarevic to give direct orders to MUP without them first of all receiving instructions in relation to resubordination from a superior MUP organ?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A MUP unit would not be subordinated to General Lazarevic without first receiving an order from its own superior. It will cooperate and coordinate, but it will not be resubordinated unless it receives a specific order from its own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how would that normally be arranged?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of the interior issues an order to the MUP staff or to its superior body, he issues a written order whereby his own forces which are in the areas of combat of the army are resubordinated to the army commanders. And that order is sent down the chain of command until it reaches the unit commanders, and in that case General Lazarevic and army commanders are authorised to issue orders to MUP units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a general order that applies throughout the period of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order is a general order applying throughout the duration of the conflict, but the resubordination relation does not hold throughout this period but only for particular actions. The moment the action is complete, the MUP unit is no longer under the authority of the military commander until the need arises for a new anti-terrorist operation or, for example, a fight against NATO forces in a ground operation which seemed to be meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've got to excuse our direct experience of military matters, Mr. Radinovic, but that doesn't really clarify it for me. The NATO conflict lasted 78 days. Would the Milosevic resubordination order apply of every MUP unit assuming it had been relayed by the minister of the interior to units, would it have applied throughout the 78-day period or would there have been stages when renewal was required?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards that level of command, it would have applied throughout the entire period of the war. The president of the state would not have had to renew the order, nor would the minister have had to do so, it wouldn't have been done at the highest levels. But the command bodies on the ground, organizing, planning, and carrying out the actions would have to bear that in mind. And every time the need arose for police forces to participate in combat operations waged by the army, they would have to order their units to join in and to be resubordinated. The operative orders at the lower level would not apply throughout the 78 days of the war because in those 78 days the police forces had different duties to carry out, not just participating in military actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is the part I'm afraid I fail to understand, and it may be that questions from Mr. Ivetic or Mr. Ackerman would help me. But resubordination is meaningless if, in fact, the army commanders cannot directly command MUP forces without further intervention from some higher MUP organ, and that I do not at the moment understand. Can you assist, Mr. Ivetic? You're not obliged to. You're simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to think of a question that would perhaps have this witness answer it. I can't on the top of my head I do have a correction on the transcript page 64, line 14, the superior organ, he mentioned the RJB. That is the only advice I can at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're saying he did mention the RJB?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, the superior organ being the RJB, the Resor Javne Bezbednosti I think is what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour, and try to provide an explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you can help me, please do.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour. The high levels issue orders covering long -- longer period of time, and these orders at that level need not be renewed. They simply order resubordination, which means that in each particular action where resubordination is necessary the lower-level commanders are authorised to carry out the resubordination. But the police units which are supposed to participate in operations under the command and control of the army have to receive an order to carry this out each time. Sometimes these actions would last half a day or even less, and for each and every action they would have to receive an order to at such and such a time in such and such a place be placed under the command of the Pristina Corps until the task was completed. As soon as the task was completed, they would go back to their regular duties until there was a new action, and this would be repeated every time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a question, General, to ask here. When the NATO action started, did the president of Yugoslavia address the nation and pass certain orders, like presidents do in the event of an emergency? Did he explain certain things? Did he address the nation or didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not address the nation, but the nation was fully aware of all this. This had been imminent for quite some time and the nation was quite aware of it. There were plans for the use of the army, there was a war plan, there were plans of engagement, and for these initial operational plans, no special order was required. The use of the army in possible war situations had been planned, and various scenarios of the imposed war were considered for months beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The president did not address the nation during the entire crucial period? Didn't he address the nation at all explaining things? No?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the beginning of the war, no, he did not. Well, he did address the nation from time to time, of course, and the public followed his activities as head of stated and in the peace negotiations, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were assisting me and I return to the point I was -- sorry, Mr. Ackerman, you wished to intervene there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just -- I think maybe to clarify something, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I complete what I was trying to do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because I hadn't finished what I was asking. I think I'm getting clearer now. You're saying that at the Lazarevic level, once the task was completed if he wanted to engage MUP forces again there would require to be a further order, that's an internal order within the MUP structure, requiring them to be resubordinated to the Pristina Corps. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Lazarevic level, no, because that's a high level and for him, the order he received from his army commander was sufficient. The commander of the 3rd Army ordered that MUP units be resubordinated to him and that was enough for him but it was not enough for the MUP units that were supposed to participate in the actions. They did not get orders from their own superiors to be resubordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My reason for asking the question that way was in your answer you said but the police units which are to participate in operations under the command and control of the VJ have to receive an order to carry this out each time. Sometimes these actions would last half a day or even less, and for each and every one they would have to receive an order to at such and such a time and in such and such a place be placed under the command of the Pristina Corps until the task was completed. As soon as the task was completed they would go back to their regular duties until there was a new action. So I wrongly assumed that you were talking about the commander of the Pristina Corps level when you said that. So tell me at what level the resubordination would be for a task and would have to be rearranged for the next task, at what level would that kick in?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level at which the action was being carried out. Throughout the war the Pristina Corps never carried out a corps operation involving all the forces of the whole corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could that then apply at brigade level?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How would the brigade commander go about arranging for an instruction to be given to the appropriate MUP organs that they were to be resubordinated to him for a particular task?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area, it's the same area where the MUP units and the army units are, they are in the same area. And according to the action envisaged he planned his own forces and he planned those police forces who were in the area. And he issued them with tasks in line with their equipment, training, purpose, and their combat and other abilities. But the order to the commander of the police unit which was supposed to participate in the action had to be issued to him by his own superior, he had to be told by his own superior that he should be resubordinated to the army commander. Otherwise, subordination in combat actions is not a permanent category because this was only a minor, although very important, part of their duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The logic of this, I'm afraid, defeats me. There must be a point in the MUP structure where the VJ officer is commanding a MUP officer to give directions to his inferiors. How is it he does that? Does he ask them kindly to do it so the control of this is in the hands of MUP officer, or does the army officer have the authority to say, Look, you tell those in the following units that they have to follow my orders for this operation? How is that done?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's done according to the system of coordination. The MUP staff at Kosovo and the Pristina Corps had to coordinate. They would agree on their mutual relations, and at these mutual coordination meetings they would decide which MUP units would participate in combat activities. I'm sure that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But surely, Mr. Radinovic, that gives the ultimate power to the MUP staff to say, Get lost, we'll do it our way?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, if the order did not reach them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now we're getting to it I think. Mr. Ackerman, is there anything else you want to ask about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think maybe perspective could be important. The Milosevic order was issued on the 18th of April, so that would have been the beginning of the effort to resubordinate the MUP. The 18th of April was the 26th of those 78 days, and by that time the vast majority of the crime base in the indictment had already occurred. So we're talking about a fairly minimal number of crime-based events that happened after the 18th of April, and I think getting it in that perspective might help a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree entirely, but I still have in my mind an earlier answer that Article 16 and 17 apply automatically, you don't actually require an order from the president to trigger this whole system, all you need is a declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there's evidence - and I can't tell you the documents right now - where there's complaint that -- there's refusal to resubordinate and things like that on behalf of certain MUP units. I think the thing that might be difficult to get our minds around is that these kinds of things happened at a very low tactical level, this is out in the field where the battle is going on and who is commanding the action in the field. You have two commanders in a field, a MUP commander and an army commander or do you have one commander commanding both forces. When you have a resubordination one commander commands both forces. The understanding that I have is that never happened in this situation, but it never happens at a level up as high as Lazarevic, you're two or three levels above the tactical level at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it -- Let me ask Mr. Radinovic just finally to clarify it. Assume that Milosevic had never made that order and a brigade commander decided that he wanted to have the assistance of MUP forces to carry out a particular task and he got the cooperation of the MUP staff, am I right in understanding that Articles 16 and 17 would allow him then to have the MUP forces resubordinated to him for that task on the basis of an order issued by the MUP staff to their inferior units?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been quite enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think that's as much as we can do today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One correction in the transcript, line 70 -- pardon, page 70, line 17, the witness said: Unfortunately, yes, if the order didn't reach them and the last part of that did not make it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radinovic, we will need to stop there for today and tomorrow morning at 9.00 we'll start with the cross-examination by the Prosecutor. It would obviously be helpful if you would undertake the further research you said you would in the course of this afternoon, and in fact perhaps the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in my notes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first thing to do tomorrow will be to tell the results of that research before we begin the cross-examination by Mr. Stamp . Meanwhile, please bear in mind that even though you are doing research and you are making further inquiries for your own purposes, it's vital that you do not have any communication about the evidence with anyone in the case. No one's entitled to speak to you about the evidence, and you're not entitled to speak to anyone about the evidence while you're in the witness box. So until your evidence is complete you may talk to people about things other than the evidence. Now, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and return ready to recommence at 9.00 a.m. tomorrow.
